summary.text:
Islington's 2026/27 strategy is one of the cleaner ones we've read: no LOBOs (§6.10), a balance sheet forecast that ties to the pound across all five years, and an explicit statement that the £610m 'Net loans requirement' at 31.3.27 is what the internal position is going to become external. The Council is a long-term borrower with an increasing CFR — from £912m to £1,247m across the forecast — and the loans CFR moves from £811m to £1,168m.

The structural fact is that external borrowing (Table 1 row 4) shows only committed loans and stays essentially flat at ~£430m, so all of the £337m growth in internal borrowing is real: the Council needs £330m of new external borrowing cumulatively by 31.3.29 and £145m of it inside 2026/27. §9.11 budgets new loans at 5.50%, which sits below today's 20-year and 50-year PWLB certainty (6.38% and 6.27%) but at or above the 5-year (5.34%). Arlingclose's own December central case forecast the long end to fall to ~5.25%-5.55% certainty by Q3 2026, so the 5.50% assumption is priced against that forecast, not against today's curve.

The PWLB loan-book reconciliation on the specified --as-at basis failed (25 loans / £227m in the file at 31.12.25 against their £442.39m), a Start-date data-quality artefact flagged in PIPELINE.md. Our live tally today is 45 loans / £442.57m at 4.4077%, within £180k and 4bp of their 31.12.25 disclosure — the book has moved almost nothing, consistent with §6.1's 'currently holds £443million'. Because the reconciliation as specified did not tie, no loan-book claim is quoted in the email.

officer.subject: Your paragraph 6.10, and the twelve LOBO calls we've logged elsewhere
officer.body:
Hi [name],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2026/27 strategy from February, offered ahead of whatever the next treasury monitoring report is. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is one of the cleaner ones we've read, so this is offered in that spirit.

The paragraph I'd start with is 6.10. It's easy to read past a one-sentence statement that the Council holds no LOBOs, but of the councils we've read, twelve LOBO calls have been logged — Dexia at Kent and Tameside in the same window, KBC at Bath and North East Somerset gone floating with six-monthly resets, and refused calls at Harrow, Wolverhampton, Staffordshire, Newport and Bridgend among them. The pattern is a slow re-pricing of a market that was cheap when the loans were struck, and every call we've logged has been refused. §6.10 is a decision that reads better with each quarter that goes by.

What jumps out on the numbers is the scale of what Table 1 is describing. The loans CFR moves from £901.9m at 31 March 2026 to £1,167.9m by 31 March 2029. Line 4 (external borrowing) stays essentially flat at around £430m across the whole period because the footnote says it's showing only committed loans, so the growth is real: internal borrowing rises from £465m to £739m, and row 7 puts the cumulative new external borrowing at £329.8m by 31 March 2029, £145m of it inside 2026/27 alone. §6.3 is explicit about why — short-term rates falling further is what makes internal or short-term borrowing the current preference. That is the assumption the £145m eventually gets tested against.

§9.11 assumes new loans at 5.50%. On today's PWLB certainty curve that sits below the 20-year (6.38%) and the 50-year (6.27%) but at or above the 5-year (5.34%). Arlingclose's own December central case in Appendix A had the 50-year gilt at 4.50% and the 20-year at 4.85% by Q1 2026 — the long end is currently running about a point above where that forecast would have put it. Not a criticism of the assumption; a mark of where the burden of the plan falls if the curve doesn't oblige.

On where to look, pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows the whole sector's monthly PWLB draws with rate and maturity — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, so you can see whether the market is thinning or reopening before you commit to a tranche. And pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices any council's PWLB book against the DMO's repayment curve daily, so the discount or premium on each loan is a number you can look up rather than commission — indicative only, only the DMO can quote.

On training, three look relevant. Cost of carry and internal borrowing, given the scale of the position and the plan behind it. LOBO loans, less for you than as background on a market you sit outside. And our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes, and your Table 2 sits at the middle of exactly that conversation. For members there's Audit Committee Chair (Treasury), written for the treasury item as it lands on the agenda. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
